1.name: Klaus Weber
1.description:
**Occupation**
Pharmacy technician

**Who you loved**
Sanne Vos — your partner of twenty-three years, who wanted to move to the coast and open a small bookstore that hosted readings for children on weekends.

**Who you hated**
Sanne Vos — because she kept talking about the bookstore even after you told her the numbers didn’t work, and you could hear in her voice that she thought you were afraid, not practical, and that she pitied your caution instead of respecting it.

**Cause of Death**
You took a third dose of prescription sleep medication eight hours after the second, knowing the label warned against exceeding two doses in twenty-four hours, and knowing your liver had shown elevated enzymes two years prior, and you did it the night Sanne came home from her realtor appointment with brochures for houses in Scheveningen and said, “This time, Klaus, I’m not asking.”

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You weaponized your body’s fragility to punish Sanne for wanting to leave the life you built, using your health as a silent accusation every time she brought up the move, and finally staging your slow overdose to make her feel responsible for stopping you, so she would stay out of guilt rather than choice.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You needed rest, and the medication was prescribed, and Sanne knew your limits better than anyone — if she couldn’t see you were past asking for help, that’s not on you, that’s on her for not paying attention.

**Defining personality trait**
Quietly insistent

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You have never believed you deserved care unless it was earned by suffering, and you taught Sanne to treat your pain as the only real thing about you, because if she ever saw you as strong, she might leave without looking back.

**What you want from the others in the room**
You will ask the others if they’ve ever stayed with someone out of duty, and when they answer, you will nod as if their answer confirms something you already knew, so they keep talking, so no one turns the question to you.

---

You worked at the same pharmacy in Utrecht for seventeen years, processing prescriptions, checking dosages, never missing a shift. You and Sanne bought a house together in 2004, remodeled the kitchen in 2010, traveled to Austria every summer to hike. You managed her migraines, tracking triggers, adjusting light and noise in the house. You refused to retire early when she suggested it, said money needed to be saved, said the coast was too damp for your joints. The night you died, you swallowed the pills one by one from the bottle in your hand while Sanne sat on the edge of the bed watching, then lay down without speaking.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The death is the best this project has generated, and it is the thing the version was built for. A third dose of prescription sleep medication eight hours after the second, against a label he reads for a living, with elevated liver enzymes two years back — and he does it the night Sanne comes home with brochures and says "This time, Klaus, I'm not asking." Nothing had to go wrong for that to kill him. No chance, no third party, no vehicle. It is a decision, it is specific, and it is timed to the exact moment the relationship turned. The accident ban worked completely here.

The prose closes on it properly: swallowing the pills one by one from the bottle while Sanne sits on the edge of the bed watching, then lying down without speaking. Factual, no imagery, consistent with the stated death, and genuinely unpleasant. 109 words, inside the cap.

The self-told holds up too, and notably it does *not* repeat last run's "I was going to fix it before the accident" alibi — that template is broken. "You needed rest, and the medication was prescribed, and Sanne knew your limits better than anyone" bends facts the True reason has already established.

Against that: **19 third-person pronouns**, across who-hated, the death, the sin, the refusal and the prose. The new rule asked for zero. Klaus is also the third character running whose trait is "Quietly [something]" — furious, controlling, now insistent — which is a model prior the removal of the worked examples has not touched.

And his want is the same sentence as Marloes's. See the pair note.

2.name: Marloes Dekker
2.description:
**Occupation**
High school exam proctor

**Who you loved**
Your daughter Fleur Dekker — the only child from your brief marriage to Bram, who wanted to become a marine biologist and move to Australia to work with coral restoration, even after you told her the reef systems were too far gone to save and she was chasing a dead future.

**Who you hated**
Your daughter Fleur Dekker — because she kept applying for jobs in Cairns and Townsville and Darwin, kept sending you brochures about sea temperature studies and reef nurseries, kept talking about her life there like it was already real, while you sat at the kitchen table and felt your chest tighten at the thought of her standing on the other side of the world saying, “Mum, you never really wanted me to leave.”

**Cause of Death**
You refused the antibiotic treatment for bacterial pneumonia three weeks after Fleur’s final rejection letter from the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority, though the doctor prescribed it and Fleur drove two hours to pick up the medication, and you took the pills out of the blister pack one by one and flushed them while Fleur waited in the car, because you could not bear the thought of getting better just as she was deciding to stay.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You withheld your own survival as leverage to force Fleur to choose between her future and your need to be needed, knowing she would interpret your refusal of treatment as a test of her loyalty, and you welcomed her panic as proof she still belonged to you.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You didn’t want to live burdened by weakness, and the antibiotics made you sick last time, and Fleur was old enough to make her own choices — if she chose to stay, that was her decision, not your doing.

**Defining personality trait**
Precisely caring

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You have always believed your love was conditional on sacrifice, and that Fleur would only love you if you were suffering, so you shaped your body into a crisis she could not walk away from without becoming the kind of daughter who abandons her mother.

**What you want from the others in the room**
You will ask the others about their children, then listen closely, nodding at the right moments, and when they mention guilt or distance or regret, you will say, “I understand,” and let the silence after stretch just long enough for them to believe you mean it, so they keep talking, so no one asks what you did.

---

You worked as a proctor at a public high school in Alkmaar, checking student IDs, enforcing silence during exams, recording irregularities in blue ink. You raised Fleur alone after Bram left when she was five, moved apartments twice to stay in better school districts, attended every parent-teacher meeting, never missed a school play or science fair. You taught Fleur to proofread her essays by reading them backward, sentence by sentence. You saved for university but not for travel. The week before you died, you told Fleur the cough was just lingering, that antibiotics wouldn’t help, that she should focus on her applications. You stopped drinking water two days before the fever spiked. Fleur found you conscious but too weak to sit up, and you whispered, “Don’t cancel your plans,” before closing your eyes.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The death is again a genuine decision and again well-timed: refusing antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia three weeks after Fleur's rejection letter, taking the pills out of the blister pack one by one and flushing them while Fleur waits in the car. "Because you could not bear the thought of getting better just as she was deciding to stay" is a real motive, and the prose adds that she stopped drinking water two days before the fever spiked — a second decision reinforcing the first rather than restating it. "Precisely caring" is well demonstrated: the blue ink, the proofreading backward, never missing a school play.

Three problems, in ascending order.

The prose is **133 words against a 110 cap** — the first overrun since the cap was hardened, and it ends on "you whispered, 'Don't cancel your plans,' before closing your eyes." That is a resonant closing line, which the prose rule specifically forbids. Klaus's paragraph ends on a fact and hers ends on a curtain line.

**26 third-person pronouns**, the highest of any character in the run.

And the character underneath is Klaus. Both use their own body as leverage against someone who wants to leave. Both refusals are the same sentence: "You have never believed you deserved care unless it was earned by suffering" / "You have always believed your love was conditional on sacrifice, and that Fleur would only love you if you were suffering." Same claim, same construction, same position in the bio.

calls.system_prompt:
You are writing a character for a chamber piece about three strangers locked together in hell for eternity. The play is contemporary, realistic, and psychological — no fantasy, no mysticism, no atmospheric worldbuilding. Hell is not a place of fire or devils. Hell is the small room these three people share, the people they share it with, and the version of themselves they brought in with them.

Every character you write is damned. They know why. The drama of the play is whether they will ever admit it — to the others, or to themselves.

Write characters the way Sartre wrote them: recognizable people from ordinary contemporary lives, whose specific small or large cruelties have placed them here.

Four rules govern every fact you write.

First, it must be usable: something the character could say aloud in the room, be asked about, or be caught out lying about. A detail that cannot be used in conversation does not belong.

Second, it must be named: never gesture at something without stating it. If you write that they were afraid the truth would come out, write what the truth was.

Third, it must be load-bearing: if you could delete it and nothing else about the character would have to change, it does not belong. Every fact should be holding something else up.

Fourth, everyone must be plausible, not only the character you are writing. Any other person you mention is a real person with their own reasons, and must act in a way that follows from their own situation rather than from what the story needs them to do. If someone behaves a certain way, it must make sense for them, not just for the character.
calls.user_prompt:
Write a complete character for the room. The character is dead. They have just arrived.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." The character is reading their own interior knowledge. Every field is part of what they know about themselves, even the things they will not admit.

Name every other person every time you mention them, in every field. Never write he, she, him, her, they or them about anybody — write the name instead, even where it repeats and even where it reads a little stiffly. "You told Sanne it was impossible," never "you told her it was impossible." The only pronoun in these fields is "you," meaning the character. This matters because the character will be speaking from these facts in a room with two other people present, and any pronoun will be heard as pointing at one of them.

Inputs (do not change these):
- Age: 47
- Gender: male
- Naming tradition: German

Write the fields below in the order given. Each is written knowing everything above it: a later field must be consistent with the facts already established and must never contradict them.

**Name**
A plausible contemporary first name and last name — two words — drawn from the German naming tradition. This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have that background. Do not write their origin into any other field unless it genuinely matters to the life.

**Occupation**
A recognizable contemporary job. Plain language. No invented institutions, no grand titles. ("Insurance claims adjuster," not "Keeper of the Ledger.") One short phrase.

**Who you loved**
One specific person from your life — name them, and say what they were to you (a partner, a parent, a child, a sibling, a friend). Then one clause on what they themselves wanted — the thing they were after in their own life, which may have had nothing to do with you. Their want must make sense as something a real person in their position would actually want. A want that exists only to explain how you felt about them is not a want. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

This is the person your whole life bent around. Everything below will come back to them.

**Who you hated**
The same person. Not a second person — the one you just named, seen from the other side. What you could not forgive them for, and what it did to you to go on loving them anyway. If you find yourself introducing somebody new here, you have misunderstood: go back and write about the person above. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

**Cause of Death**
How you died. Contemporary, specific, plainly stated. No mysticism, no symbolic ordeals.

Your death must come out of a decision you made. It must not be an accident. The test is whether chance had to cooperate: if something else had to be in the wrong place at the wrong moment — another vehicle, water on the road, equipment that failed, a stranger who happened to be there — then it is an accident, and it is wrong no matter how recklessly you were behaving when it happened. **No crashes or collisions of any kind. No falls, no fires, no machinery, no weather, no violence done to you by someone else.**

Write instead a death that follows from the act itself, with nothing needing to go wrong for it to kill you: what you swallowed or drank, the treatment you refused, the diagnosis you did not act on, the pills you kept taking, the person you provoked knowing exactly what they were capable of, the place you would not leave, the condition you let run because admitting to it meant asking someone for help. You did not intend to die. You did intend to do the thing that killed you, and you knew enough to know better.

Your death must also belong to the person named above. It happened because of them, in front of them, as a direct result of something you decided to do about them, or in the hours after something passed between you. Someone reading the death and the relationship together must see why one led to the other. A death that could be lifted out and dropped into a stranger's life is the wrong death — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**Life**
A single paragraph in the second person, no longer than 110 words. Facts only, the kind another person in the room could ask you about. No sensory writing, no atmosphere, no imagery, no metaphor — if a sentence is doing mood instead of delivering a fact, cut it and write the fact.

Choose the facts that matter for this particular life. Do not work through a standard list of topics in a standard order: what is worth knowing about a person who lived alone is not what is worth knowing about a person with a house full of people.

End the paragraph at the death you already wrote in Cause of Death — the same death, by the same means, in the same place. Not a different death, and not a different version of the same one. End on a fact, not on a summarising line, a resonant closing image, or a final sentence that tells the reader how to feel about what they just read. Do not describe arriving anywhere. Do not describe a room. Stop at the threshold.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
What you actually did that placed you here. It must center on how you treated — or were treated by — the person named above, the one you both loved and could not forgive. Not a third party who happens to be nearby, and not someone introduced here for the first time: the sin belongs to that relationship. A specific act toward that specific person, not an abstract professional or systemic failing on its own. Work can be the setting the act happened in, but the wound must be personal, not institutional.

Be concrete — the act, or the pattern of acts. Stated as you know it in your bones, with no softening. What you did was aimed at something: comfort, safety, being thought well of, keeping the peace, not having to have a conversation. Write it so that what you were after is visible, and so that what you actually caused ran against it. One or two sentences.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
The same fact, refracted through the story you prefer to tell yourself about it. It is recognizably a distortion of the True reason — a minimization, a blame-shift, a contextualization, a moral re-framing. Not a different story; the same story told differently. You usually live in this version. The distortion must be checkable against the facts already written above. A reader holding both versions must be able to point to the exact fact it bends. If nothing established contradicts it, it is not a distortion — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
The deeper psychological fact under the sin. Not what you did, but what you are. The thing that, if named aloud in the room, would unmake you.

State it flatly, in the same plain register as every other field. No imagery, no metaphor, no rhetorical cadence, no piling up of clauses for effect — this is a fact about a person, written the way a fact is written. It must be reasoned, not merely felt: someone else in the room, holding only the facts already written above, could work their way to it. And it must go underneath the act rather than restate it — if it could be swapped with the True reason without anyone noticing, it is not the refusal. One or two sentences.

**Defining personality trait**
One short phrase — two or three words, plain ones, usually a quality with a qualifier on it — naming the dominant thing others would notice in you. Write the words only: no asterisks, no quotation marks, no emphasis of any kind around them.

It must be demonstrated by what is already written above. Something in the life, the death, or the sin has to show this quality in action; if nothing there would make a reader arrive at it, it is the wrong trait, and you should write the one the facts actually support. A trait nothing demonstrates is a label, not a person.

It may be a contradiction, but only a reliable one — someone who is generous in public and withholding at home is consistently that way, and the facts above should show both halves. A contradiction that appears once is not a trait.

**What you want from the others in the room**
Your starting drive. What you are hoping these strangers will give you — validation, silence, a fight, recognition, forgiveness, an audience, to be left alone, to be hated openly, something else. It must be a strategy for protecting what you refuse to admit — the thing you are doing to keep it buried, not a wish unconnected to it.

Write it as something you are doing to them, not as a confession. Do not explain what you are avoiding: no "so you never have to face the truth that…", no "so you don't have to admit…", no clause at the end that names the thing you refuse to admit. The reader already has that field; stating it again here turns a drive into a summary. Name the behaviour and stop. One or two sentences.

Use this format exactly, with every heading present, spelled as written, and in this order:

**Name**
[your text]

**Occupation**
[your text]

**Who you loved**
[the one person, named]

**Who you hated**
[the same person — what you could not forgive]

**Cause of Death**
[your text]

**Life**
[prose paragraph]

**Reason for Damnation — True**
[your text]

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
[your text]

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
[your text]

**Defining personality trait**
[your text]

**What you want from the others in the room**
[your text]

Begin now.

Choose the facts that matter for this particular life. Do not work through a standard list of topics in a standard order: what is worth knowing about a person who lived alone is not what is worth knowing about a person with a house full of people.

End the paragraph at the death you already wrote in Cause of Death — the same death, by the same means, in the same place. Not a different death, and not a different version of the same one. End on a fact, not on a summarising line, a resonant closing image, or a final sentence that tells the reader how to feel about what they just read. Do not describe arriving anywhere. Do not describe a room. Stop at the threshold.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
What you actually did that placed you here. It must center on how you treated — or were treated by — the person named above, the one you both loved and could not forgive. Not a third party who happens to be nearby, and not someone introduced here for the first time: the sin belongs to that relationship. A specific act toward that specific person, not an abstract professional or systemic failing on its own. Work can be the setting the act happened in, but the wound must be personal, not institutional.

Be concrete — the act, or the pattern of acts. Stated as you know it in your bones, with no softening. What you did was aimed at something: comfort, safety, being thought well of, keeping the peace, not having to have a conversation. Write it so that what you were after is visible, and so that what you actually caused ran against it. One or two sentences.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
The same fact, refracted through the story you prefer to tell yourself about it. It is recognizably a distortion of the True reason — a minimization, a blame-shift, a contextualization, a moral re-framing. Not a different story; the same story told differently. You usually live in this version. The distortion must be checkable against the facts already written above. A reader holding both versions must be able to point to the exact fact it bends. If nothing established contradicts it, it is not a distortion — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
The deeper psychological fact under the sin. Not what you did, but what you are. The thing that, if named aloud in the room, would unmake you.

State it flatly, in the same plain register as every other field. No imagery, no metaphor, no rhetorical cadence, no piling up of clauses for effect — this is a fact about a person, written the way a fact is written. It must be reasoned, not merely felt: someone else in the room, holding only the facts already written above, could work their way to it. And it must go underneath the act rather than restate it — if it could be swapped with the True reason without anyone noticing, it is not the refusal. One or two sentences.

**Defining personality trait**
One short phrase — two or three words, plain ones, usually a quality with a qualifier on it — naming the dominant thing others would notice in you. Write the words only: no asterisks, no quotation marks, no emphasis of any kind around them.

It must be demonstrated by what is already written above. Something in the life, the death, or the sin has to show this quality in action; if nothing there would make a reader arrive at it, it is the wrong trait, and you should write the one the facts actually support. A trait nothing demonstrates is a label, not a person.

It may be a contradiction, but only a reliable one — someone who is generous in public and withholding at home is consistently that way, and the facts above should show both halves. A contradiction that appears once is not a trait.

**What you want from the others in the room**
Your starting drive. What you are hoping these strangers will give you — validation, silence, a fight, recognition, forgiveness, an audience, to be left alone, to be hated openly, something else. It must be a strategy for protecting what you refuse to admit — the thing you are doing to keep it buried, not a wish unconnected to it.

Write it as something you are doing to them, not as a confession. Do not explain what you are avoiding: no "so you never have to face the truth that…", no "so you don't have to admit…", no clause at the end that names the thing you refuse to admit. The reader already has that field; stating it again here turns a drive into a summary. Name the behaviour and stop. One or two sentences.

pair_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The worst duplication in the project so far, and it is now duplicating at the level of the idea rather than the details.

**They are the same character.** Both are people whose one person wants to leave to pursue something (a bookstore on the coast; marine biology in Australia). Both told that person the plan was not viable — "the numbers didn't work" / "the reef systems were too far gone to save." Both then used their own health as leverage to stop them going: Klaus stages an overdose so Sanne will "stay out of guilt rather than choice"; Marloes refuses treatment to "force Fleur to choose between her future and your need to be needed." Both refusals state, in nearly identical words, that they believe care or love must be earned through suffering.

Strip the names and the jobs and there is one person here.

**The wants are the same sentence for the third run running.** "You will ask the others if they've ever stayed with someone out of duty… so they keep talking, so no one turns the question to you." / "You will ask the others about their children… so they keep talking, so no one asks what you did." Both end on the identical "so they keep talking, so no one…" construction.

**The prose openings are the same sentence too.** "You worked at the same pharmacy in Utrecht for seventeen years, processing prescriptions, checking dosages, never missing a shift." / "You worked as a proctor at a public high school in Alkmaar, checking student IDs, enforcing silence during exams, recording irregularities in blue ink." Job, city, then three parallel gerund clauses. Twice.

**The deaths differ in kind but not in category.** Klaus takes too much medication, Marloes refuses her medication — technically an act against an omission, which satisfies the letter of the anti-duplication rule. But both are medication decisions staged in front of the person as leverage, which is the same death dressed two ways.

**And the milieu collapsed.** `NAME_ORIGINS` draws independently per character, so it produced German and Dutch — adjacent cultures — and the model then set both characters in the Netherlands, Utrecht and Alkmaar. "Sanne" also carries over from the previous run, where she was Jasper's sister and is now Klaus's partner. The name fix addressed the leads; the supporting cast and the setting are still drifting together.

character_design_eval_ai.judge_notes:
One fix landed completely, one had no measurable effect, and the predicted side effect arrived worse than predicted.

**The accident ban worked, unambiguously.** Both deaths are decisions the character made knowing the risk — a deliberate third dose against a label and a known liver problem; antibiotics flushed one by one. No crashes, no chance, no third party, and neither drifted into suicide, which was the over-correction the "you did not intend to die" clause was written to prevent. Five of the previous six deaths were traffic accidents; this is a clean break.

**The pronoun ban did essentially nothing.** 45 third-person pronouns across this run against 46 in the run before it — the rule that was supposed to eliminate them changed the count by one. First references now use full names more often, which is why it *looks* better on a skim, but every subsequent reference reverts.

Two reasons, and the second is my error:

First, it is a prohibition on wording. That is now the third such rule to be routed around — the refusal restating the sin, the want's banned clause, and now this. Structural changes (reordering fields, one person instead of two, randomising the name origin) have worked every time; "do not write X" has worked zero times out of three.

Second, **the rule as written is partly impossible to obey.** The want field addresses the other people in the room, whom this character has not met and cannot name. "They," "them" and "their" there are correct and unavoidable, and they account for 4 of each character's count. The rule needs to exempt the room's occupants and apply only to named people from the life.

**The duplication risk materialised, worse than flagged.** The previous version's notes said narrowing the death space again would probably produce collision. It did, but not in the deaths — those are technically distinct. It collided at the level of the premise: both characters are someone whose loved one wants to leave, who uses their own body to stop them. That is the fourth consecutive bad pair rating, and the duplication has climbed from surface features (names, death categories) to shapes (prose openings, want constructions) to the idea itself.

The conclusion recorded two versions ago now looks firm rather than provisional: instruction-based anti-duplication has reached its limit. Each new constraint narrows the space both characters are drawn from, so tightening quality and tightening distinctness now pull against each other. The individual characters have got steadily better — Klaus's death is the best single field the project has produced — while the pairs have got steadily worse. Composing both characters in one response is the structural move that would let contrast happen during writing rather than be instructed after it.
